title: Why China needs Russia more than you think
gist: The consensus that Beijing dominates Moscow because Russia sends 34 percent of its trade to China while China sends only four percent to Russia is analytically wrong: Beijing values Russia through a Cold-War-style strategic triangle in which Moscow is the only major power outside the US orbit, supplying 17 percent of China's oil imports and 30 percent of its gas, a 5,500-warhead deterrent, a quiet land border, and gatekeeper access to Central Asia and the Arctic. Russia's leverage over China therefore rises, not falls, as US-China rivalry intensifies.

themes.theme: The strategic triangle as Beijing's operating frame

insights.claim: Chinese analysts frame Beijing-Moscow ties through 'triangular relations' with Washington, a deliberate revival of the Cold War strategic triangle in which the 1970s logic is inverted: instead of Beijing and Washington balancing Moscow, Beijing now cultivates Moscow to counterbalance Washington.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese policy toward Russia should be modelled as a function of US-China tension, not of bilateral economics — meaning any US-China escalation mechanically raises Beijing's willingness to underwrite Moscow.
insights.quote: Whereas in the 1970s, Beijing and Washington drew closer to counter-balance Moscow, today, Beijing cultivates Moscow as a counterweight to Washington.
insights.locator: Chinese analysts often frame China-Russia relations

insights.claim: The conventional wisdom that Beijing dominates the relationship because Russia depends on China economically is explicitly wrong, even though Russia routes at least 34 percent of its global trade through China while Russia is only around four percent of China's two-way trade and China's GDP is roughly eight times Russia's.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Trade-share asymmetry is the most commonly cited proof of Chinese leverage and is being argued to be a false indicator — positioning built on 'Beijing will restrain Moscow' assumptions is mispriced.
insights.quote: But this prevailing view is wrong.
insights.locator: Conventional wisdom holds that Beijing dominates

insights.claim: Russia's value to China rests on a combination no other power can replicate — geopolitical weight, strategic geography, natural resources and a congruent anti-Western worldview — which is why its bargaining position survives its economic weakness.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China cannot substitute Russia with a friendlier or richer partner, which caps how much pressure Beijing will ever apply over Ukraine or sanctions compliance.
insights.quote: Russia’s geopolitical weight, strategic geography, natural resources and a congruent anti-Western worldview are of immense value to China when dealing with the US. No other great power has the same potent mix.

insights.claim: Moscow's worth to Beijing as the third point of a geostrategic triangle is forecast to increase as US-China rivalry intensifies, making the relationship counter-cyclical to Western pressure.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Attempts to split Beijing from Moscow by raising the cost of the partnership are likely to backfire — escalation raises Russia's price rather than lowering Chinese demand.
insights.quote: Moscow’s value as the third point in a geostrategic triangle will only increase if US-China rivalry intensifies.

themes.theme: Hard assets Russia brings to the table

insights.claim: Russia holds roughly 5,500 nuclear warheads — nine times China's arsenal — plus a large conventional military and arms manufacturing base, giving Moscow strategic weight wholly disconnected from its ninth-place GDP ranking.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: The nuclear ratio is the core reason economic dependency does not translate into political subordination — a structural floor under Russian bargaining power.
insights.quote: Moscow has a nuclear arsenal with roughly 5,500 warheads, nine times as many as China
insights.locator: Additionally, Moscow has a nuclear arsenal

insights.claim: In 2025 Russian crude supplied 17 percent of China's oil imports and Russian natural gas 30 percent of its gas imports, making Moscow a first-order input to Chinese energy security rather than a marginal supplier.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A 30 percent gas share means any disruption to Russian supply is a Chinese industrial-cost shock — Beijing has a direct commercial stake in keeping the flows and the regime stable.
insights.quote: In 2025, Russian crude accounted for 17% of China’s oil imports and Russian natural gas for 30% of its gas imports.
insights.locator: Russia also holds vast oil and gas reserves

insights.claim: Russia's status as a major grain producer and exporter matters to a China that is import-dependent on both energy and grains and actively seeking to diversify away from concentrated supply sources.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Food security is an underweighted pillar of the relationship — expect Russian agricultural market access in China to expand as a political deliverable.
insights.quote: With China dependent upon imported energy and grains and eager to diversify its sources of supply, Russian exports of these strategic commodities are valuable to Beijing.
insights.locator: Moreover, its agricultural sector is substantial

insights.claim: Russia retains institutional heft as a permanent UN Security Council member and as a core partner in Sinocentric forums including BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Russia is the multilateral force-multiplier for Beijing's alternative-order project; sidelining Moscow would hollow out the institutions China is investing in.
insights.locator: While no longer the superpower it was

insights.claim: Russia is a rarity for Beijing — a large neighbor sharing an extended land border that is both peaceful and free of territorial disputes, in a periphery China otherwise perceives as saturated with traditional and nontraditional threats.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: A quiet northern border is what frees Chinese military planning and force posture to concentrate on maritime and Indo-Pacific contingencies.
insights.quote: making Russia a rarity – a non-threatening neighbor in a neighborhood Beijing perceives as teeming with traditional and nontraditional threats
insights.locator: Geography also makes Russia particularly valuable to China

insights.claim: Russia functions as gatekeeper to two regions of rising strategic importance for China: landlocked Central Asia and the Arctic maritime domain, where Russia's northern coast anchors a sea route running from the Pacific to the Atlantic.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Chinese access to Arctic shipping and Central Asian corridors is conditional on Russian consent — a lever Moscow can price, and a reason to watch Arctic route agreements as a barometer of the relationship.
insights.quote: This makes Moscow a gatekeeper to two regions of growing strategic importance: the vital landlocked expanse of Central Asia and the growing maritime domain of the Arctic.
insights.locator: Russia remains a key player in Central Asia

themes.theme: Alignment of worldview and the failure of alliance defection

insights.claim: Russia is the only permanent UN Security Council member besides China outside the US orbit and the only sizeable power that treats Washington as an implacable adversary — an antagonism that predates the war against Ukraine.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Russian anti-Americanism is structural rather than war-contingent, so a Ukraine settlement would not by itself loosen the China-Russia bloc.
insights.quote: Russia is not alone in being unhappy with Washington, but it is unique in having broken with the US-led order and embraced China as its main strategic partner.

insights.claim: The second Trump administration's combativeness toward US allies has prompted many capitals to reassess Washington as partner of choice, yet despite 'sundry humiliations' none have broken with it — Europe stays in NATO, Japan, South Korea and Australia stay core Indo-Pacific allies, and even India keeps deepening security and economic ties with Washington.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Bets on allied defection from the US system — a popular multipolarity trade — have not paid off: alliance structures have held through the stress test.
insights.quote: But despite sundry humiliations, none have yet broken with it
insights.locator: The combativeness of the second Donald Trump administration

insights.claim: Beijing and Moscow share an unusually tight ideological fit: both read the US as aggressive and meddlesome, both criticized US attacks on Iran, both see American alliances including NATO as threats, and both treat Washington as an existential danger to their respective regimes.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Regime-survival framing means the alignment is not transactional and will not be unwound by economic inducements.
insights.quote: They consider Washington intrinsically antithetical to their vital national interests, posing existential dangers to their respective regimes.
insights.locator: This has made Moscow’s worldview strikingly congruent

insights.claim: Xi Jinping's relationship with Vladimir Putin is his closest with any foreign leader, and the two have met more frequently than any other pair of sitting world leaders.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Personal leader-level capital is a real constraint on Chinese policy flexibility toward Russia for as long as both men remain in office.
insights.quote: Having met more frequently than any other two sitting world leaders, the two appear to have great respect for each other and see eye to eye on most issues.
insights.locator: On a personal level, Chinese leader Xi Jinping

insights.claim: China objects to Russia's recently expanding security ties with North Korea, regarding Pyongyang — whose economy has been overwhelmingly dependent on China for decades — as rightfully inside Beijing's sphere of influence.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: Russia-DPRK military cooperation is the clearest live wedge inside the partnership and the most likely venue for visible Sino-Russian friction.
insights.quote: China is unhappy with Russia’s recently expanding security ties with North Korea, for example, viewing Pyongyang as rightfully being within Beijing’s sphere of influence.
insights.locator: This does not mean that there are no differences of opinion

insights.claim: Beijing was unhappy with Moscow's 2022 invasion of Ukraine because the war greatly complicated China's relations with Europe and proved very disruptive to Chinese international trade — a concrete cost, not merely reputational discomfort.
insights.speaker: MERICS
insights.so_what: China bears real commercial damage from the war via the Europe relationship, which is the strongest available lever for European negotiators — but it has not been enough to change Beijing's alignment.
insights.quote: The attack and the ensuing war have greatly complicated China’s foreign relations with Europe and proved very disruptive to China’s international trade.
insights.locator: Beijing was also unhappy with Moscow’s 2022 invasion
